description: Hi! I’m Loique, AI engineer from Cameroon (Master’s in AI). We’re tackling Field Shift: NASA data + AI to help farmers adapt to climate change. Looking for data/ML fans, UI designers and a good pitcher. Agronomy students welcome. Curiosity matters more than expertise!
summary: Field Shift is a bilingual (French/English) decision-support tool that helps smallholder farmers in Cameroon’s Western Highlands choose crop rotations that protect their soil and hold up in dry years. It combines 20 years of NASA GPM IMERG rainfall and NASA POWER temperature with ISRIC SoilGrids soil data and agronomic rules from the IRAD Dschang research station. Before trusting the satellites, we checked them against 10 years of records from IRAD’s own rain gauge: GPM IMERG matched the station within 2% on total rainfall, while NASA POWER overestimated it by 32%, so we use POWER for temperature only. The engine scores every valid 2-year rotation on yield suitability, water security and soil health, weighted by the farmer’s own priorities. It compares the best three options with the farmer’s usual rotation and explains every score. On IRAD’s plot, the usual maize-beans rotation scores 85/100 but wears the soil out (65/100). Our best option scores 89/100, with soil health at 78/100. This matters because farmers in Dschang face less predictable rains and depleted soils, with no tool to compare their options.
details:
What it does
The farmer picks what matters most (yield, water security, soil health), enters the crop currently in the field and, optionally, their usual rotation and their own soil test. Field Shift evaluates every valid 2-year rotation of five local crops (maize, beans, groundnut, cassava, potato) over the two cropping seasons a year. It shows the three best options next to the farmer’s usual rotation, each with a score out of 100, its reasons, and IRAD’s practical advice. A colour band shows each season, including the dry-season periods when the soil is left bare.

How it works

  • Climate. We use 20 years (2005-2024) of GPM IMERG rainfall: the monthly product for seasonal totals, and the daily product to find the start of the rainy season each year. Temperature comes from NASA POWER.
  • Ground truth. We compared satellite rainfall with 118 months of IRAD station records (2014-2024, 2018 missing). GPM IMERG reached a monthly correlation of 0.79, with a -2% bias on total rainfall and -3% season by season. NASA POWER overestimated rainfall by 32%, so the tool uses GPM for rain and POWER only for temperature. POWER temperature is flagged as uncertain: it reads 1.3 °C warmer than the station.
  • Soil. We use ISRIC SoilGrids (pH, clay, organic carbon, 0-30 cm), or the farmer’s own soil test when they have one.
  • Local agronomy. IRAD Dschang provided each crop’s water and pH needs and sowing dates. They also gave us their rotation rules: alternate legumes with cereals or tubers, wait 3 to 4 years before the same crop returns, and never plant maize after maize or beans after groundnut.
  • Scoring. Each crop’s suitability in a season combines water (50%), temperature (25%) and soil pH (25%). The water criterion is tested year by year over the last 10 years, including the risk of a dry start after sowing and of waterlogging. Each rotation gets three scores out of 100: yield suitability, water security and soil health (nitrogen from legumes, crop families, erosion risk, IRAD rules). The final score weights them by the farmer’s priorities. Rotations that break IRAD rules are never proposed. When the farmer’s usual rotation breaks them, it is still scored, and each broken rule is shown.
  • Explanation. An AI assistant answers the farmer’s questions in plain language, using only Field Shift’s results. The server recomputes the results itself, and every number in an answer is checked against the data. If a number cannot be verified, the assistant declines to answer.

Benefits

  • The rotation advice rests on satellite data that we checked on the ground, and is tested over real years, not an average year.
  • The scores are transparent: every one comes with its reasons, so farmers and extension officers can understand and challenge them.
  • The tool respects local knowledge: IRAD’s rules are built into the engine.
  • It compares the options with what the farmer already does. On IRAD’s plot, the usual maize-beans rotation scores 85/100 but wears the soil out (65/100), while our best option scores 89/100 with soil health at 78/100.
  • It is usable on a phone, in French or English.
  • It stays a support tool. The farmer decides, and the proposals are meant to be checked with an extension officer.

Intended impact
We want farmers to protect their soil without giving up their harvest, and to plan around the real rainfall risk. In Dschang, the last decade (2015-2024) received 12% less rain than 2005-2014. The months of early growth, sowing and end of cycle (April, August, November) lost 25 to 30%. Our next steps:

  • extend Field Shift to Santchou and the Mbo plain, always after validating the data against local stations;
  • add NASA SMAP soil moisture;
  • let farmers ask questions by voice in local languages (Yemba, Pidgin) and over WhatsApp;
  • test the proposed rotations on IRAD plots with farmers.

Tools, languages and software

  • Python: pandas, xarray, earthaccess (NASA Earthdata), FastAPI, pytest, uv.
  • TypeScript: Nuxt 4, Vue 3, PrimeVue, Tailwind CSS, Chart.js, Leaflet, GSAP, @nuxtjs/i18n.
  • Infrastructure: Docker, Nginx, a Linux VPS with HTTPS.
  • AI assistant: the Anthropic API (Claude Haiku 5.5).
  • Hardware: none beyond a laptop and a server.

How the project is creative

  • We tested the satellite before trusting it. Most tools take satellite data as given. We checked two NASA sources against 10 years of local ground records, and that check changed our design: we dropped POWER for rainfall.
  • NASA data meets local agronomy. Satellite climate, a global soil map and the rules of a local research station come together in one engine.
  • The farmer’s own practice is the baseline. The tool does not only recommend; it shows how the farmer’s usual rotation compares, and which rules it breaks.
  • An AI that refuses to make things up. The assistant only sees our data, and any answer containing a number it cannot verify is blocked.

Factors we considered

  • Data accuracy: we validated rainfall on the ground, and the tool states openly what is uncertain (POWER temperature, the SoilGrids estimate of soil pH).
  • Rain-fed farming: Dschang farms without irrigation, so our water score measures whether the rain will be enough, at the right time.
  • Local knowledge: IRAD’s researchers set the agronomic rules, and we talked with 5 farmers from the area.
  • Accessibility: plain language, two languages, a phone-friendly interface, and a map of the plot.
  • Responsible AI: the assistant only explains results, never decides, and is labelled as AI.
  • Honest limits: scores measure suitability, not tonnes. For now Field Shift covers a single pilot area whose data we validated, and proposals should be checked with an extension officer.
